Observations/Recommendations 
 
ANALYSIS OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS- DEMAND NO.1 
 
ALLOCATION OF BUDGETARY RESURCES AND THEIR UTILIZATION 
 
 
1. The Committee note that the Department of Agriculture and Farmers 
Welfare has been allocated Rs. 130561.39 Crore for 2026-27 at BE stage 
whereas the Actual expenditure on Agriculture & Farmers Welfare in 2024-
25 was Rs 1,29,933.47 crore which means a hike of only around Rs 627.91 
crore or simply put a 0.5% nominal growth, over a period of two years and 
that too without factoring the rate of inflation. The actual utilization of funds 
for 2025-26 as on 31.01.2026 is Rs. 79,233.42 Crore w.r.t. RE stands at  
64.37% which clearly indicates that the Department needs to strive hard to 
fully utilize the funds in the remaining period of two months(approx.) of the 
current FY 2025-26. The Committee also note that RE of the Department for 

85  
FY 2025-26 is Rs.123,089.30 Crore which is Rs.4200.86 Crore less than its 
BE of Rs.127,290.16 Crore.  
The Committee are of the view that in case the Department is not able 
to spend the remaining funds in the last two months of FY 2025-26, there 
are high chances of not getting the enhanced allocations as sought by the 
Department, as the Ministry of Finance might take a stand that as 
surrendering of funds was done in the past, demand for allocating the 
entire amount sought by the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare 
may not be acceded to.  The Committee recommend that the Department 
may expend funds in an equitable, time-bound manner as prescribed by 
Department of Expenditure guidelines for achievement of outcome and 
output targets under various Schemes, programmes, Missions etc.  
 
The Committee recommend the Department to use real-time digital 
dashboards having Artificial Intelligence(AI) features and quarterly 
variance reviews on a regular basis  which would provide the Department 
with a real time digital oversight thereby ensuring fiscal discipline, 
transparency, and efficient delivery of public services. The Department 
must also look into issues which are pending for more than six months and 
address them which are hampering the entire spending of the allocated 

86  
amounts. The Department also needs to spruce up their Financial 
Management system as year after year the prescribed limits of Quarter wise 
spending laid down by Department of Expenditure are not being adhered 
to. The processes need to be streamlined & guidelines be amended 
accordingly, if required, to optimize utilization of funds.  
NEED FOR ENHANCEMENT OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION TO 
DEPARTMENT 
 
2. The Committee observe that the proportion of budgetary allocation 
made in favour of the Department in terms of the percentage of the total 
Central outlay for the years 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27 
stood at 3.14%, 2.57%,2.54%,2.51% and 2.44% respectively. This shows 
continuous decline in the allocations to the Department as proportion of 
Central Plan outlay. 
The Committee note that Agriculture and allied activities account for 
46.1 % of the country’s workforce but contribute only one-fifth of India’s 
national income at current prices. This disparity highlights the Agriculture 
sector's vulnerability and the urgent need for increased public investment. 
Agriculture remains the backbone of India’s growth trajectory given the fact 
that the sector   employs a large share of workforce. The Committee feel 
that investment in agriculture has a higher multiplier effect on poverty 
reduction than investment in many other sectors. Strengthening 

87  
agricultural performance is therefore important for inclusive growth, 
economic stability and ensuring food security.  
The Committee recommend that the budgetary allocation to the 
Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) is a strategic 
investment in the nation's economic sovereignty & not just a welfare 
measure and more importantly, to complement and supplement the 
overarching goal of the Union government in doubling farmers' income 
effectively. Enhanced budgetary allocation will enable the Department to 
potently counter the challenges of Climate Change, fragmented 
landholdings, increasing disruptions in global supply chains, market 
volatility and so on as these require a swift and robust financial response. 
Enhanced budgetary allocations to the Department will facilitate in its 
transition from subsistence farming to sustainable agri-business, thereby 
ensuring food security for the nation and prosperity for the Annadata (food 
provider). 
 
NEED TO ENHANCE RATE OF GROWTH IN CAPITAL FORMATION IN 
AGRICULTURE 
 
3. The Committee note that Agriculture is the backbone of our economy 
& dependence on Nature enhances the risk quotient of our Agriculture and 
this is precisely where high growth rate of Capital formation in agriculture 

88  
can effectively mitigate the risks arising due to natural calamities.  It is a 
proven fact that the growth of capital formation is a vital prerequisite for 
agricultural development.  Capital Formation in Agriculture refers to 
investment in-(i) creating physical assets such as infrastructure (ii) 
upgradation and honing of skills of human resources; and (iii) institutional 
capacity to boost productivity.  
Sustained growth in agricultural output and farmer incomes depends 
mainly on higher capital formation in agriculture. The rate of growth in 
Capital Formation in Agriculture is essential to enhance productivity as the 
most significant impact of increase in capital formation is the increase in 
yield per hectare. Growth in agricultural capital creates demand for 
industrial goods such as fertilizers, pesticides and so on. Increased 
agricultural output supplies raw materials to industries such as textiles and 
food processing. Strong infrastructure enables farmers in getting higher 
price realization for their agricultural produce. Thus, capital formation in 
agriculture acts as an engine for overall industrial growth too. 
The growth rate in Capital Formation (at current prices) in Agriculture 
and Allied Sector during the year 2019-20 was 5.1% which rose to 22.8% 
during the period 2020-21, then fell down to 15.5% in the year 2021-22, 
increased marginally during 2022-23 to 16.1% and then fell significantly to 

89  
9.6% during the period 2023-24. 
The Committee also note that the budget outlay for Agriculture & 
Farmers Welfare was Rs.1,24,000 Crore in 2022-23 whereas the total Budget 
outlay of the Union Government was Rs.39,44,908.6 Crore for the same 
period. Similarly, the budgetary allocation to Agriculture in 2026-27 BE is 
Rs. 130,561.38 Crore whereas the total budget outlay of the Union 
Government is Rs.53,47,315 Crore. Simply put, from 2022-23 to 2026-27, 
there is an increase of Rs.6561.38 Crore in Budgetary allocation for 
Agriculture and Farmers Welfare whereas the Total Budget outlay of the 
Union Government increased by Rs 14,02,406.34 Crore during the same 
period which indicates that the budgetary allocation for Agriculture did not 
get an increase in the same proportion. The Actual Expenditure in total 
Scheme Budget (Central Sector + Centrally Sponsored Schemes) of 
Agriculture in 2020-21 was Rs.1,08,090.13 Crore, out of which the  Actual 
expenditure incurred on PM-KISAN and Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima 
Yojana(PMFBY) was Rs.75151.38 Crore, which translates into Actual 
Expenditure of Rs.32938.75 Crore on other heads including creation of 
Capital Assets. This meant that around 69.53% of total Scheme Budget of 
Agriculture was spent on payment to farmers and Insurance companies 
during the period 2020-21. Similarly, the Actual Expenditure in Total 

90  
Scheme Budget (Central Sector+ Centrally Sponsored Schemes) of 
Agriculture in 2024-25 was Rs.128763.55 Crore, out of which the  Actual 
expenditure incurred on PM-KISAN and PMFBY was Rs.80594.66 Crore, 
which results into Actual Expenditure of Rs.48168.89 Crore on other heads 
including creation of Capital Assets. This meant that around 62.59% of total 
Scheme Budget of Agriculture was spent on payment to farmers and 
Insurance companies during the period 2024-25. Simply put, majority of the 
expenditure of total Scheme Budget of Agriculture goes on payments being 
made to  Farmers and Insurance companies, leaving less for investment  in 
Capital Assets and modernization of Agriculture including creating 
resilience against Climate Change.  
 The Committee recommend the Government to enhance investments 
significantly in Capital, human and institutional assets in agriculture to 
ensure that the rate of Capital Formation in Agriculture and Allied Sector 
does not come below 15% as the growth in rate of capital formation in 
agriculture is not merely an economic metric but a strategic imperative to 
ensure food security, economic stability and stimulate industrial growth.  
   
IMPORTANCE OF FARM LABOURER AND THE NEED FOR THEIR 
INCLUSION IN THE MANDATE OF DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE 
AND FARMERS WELFARE  

91  
 
4. The Committee are of the view that Farm Labourers are an important 
component of the Agricultural ecosystem in the country. Farm Labourers 
face unique & diverse challenges which are totally different than faced by 
any other class of Labourers including industrial labourers. In the current 
welfare measures being implemented by the Ministry right focus is being 
accorded for farmer welfare, but the labour which provides the necessary 
workforce in the agriculture fields is unable to reap the benefit as they do 
not own the land which they till. The Committee feel that the Department of 
Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) should make concerted efforts for 
identifying the unique challenges being faced by the labourers working on 
the farms. The Committee further note that while the   Ministry of Labour is 
the nodal Ministry to implement the welfare schemes for the labour class 
in the country, however farm labour being a distinct category and are 
different from industrial labour. As such, the agriculture labour are not 
identified as workmen/industrial labour and they are unable to reap the 
benefits being accorded to industrial labourers viz. Medical Care, Insurance 
and social Security. In this backdrop the Committee recommend that the 
Ministry Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) should consider to widen 
the ambit of component of Farmer Welfare and should include the welfare 

92  
of Farm Labourers within its scope. The Committee also recommend that 
the Ministry needs to identify programmes, schemes, missions etc for their 
inclusion in specific social security schemes such as pension funds, 
Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana, and maternity benefits tailored 
specifically for agricultural labourers.

Castes Sub Plan needs to be enhanced and procedural difficulties, if any,

ADVERTISEMENT & PUBLICITY CAMPAIGN INCLUDING USE OF DIGITAL 
PLATFORMS TO BOOST AWARENESS ABOUT ONGOING AGRICULTURAL 
SCHEMES 
 
 
7. The Committee are of the considered view that advertisement is a 
strategic initiative in bridging the information asymmetry and in ensuring 
the success of ongoing agricultural schemes. Advertisements are the 
medium through which the farmers know details of the ongoing agricultural 
schemes and their potential benefits.  There is a significant “information 
gap” between the Department and the farmers. Many farmers, especially 
those residing in remote areas, are unaware of agricultural schemes due to 
limited access to information. Publicity campaigns bridge the gap by 
disseminating information through accessible channels. Advertisement 
enhance budgetary efficiency by driving up enrolment in the ongoing 
schemes and ensuring that the allocated funds reach the intended 
beneficiaries. Agricultural schemes which are newly launched with aim to 
modernize farming need persuasive advertising campaigns to reach out to 

96  
farmers by highlighting success stories and benefits thereby reducing the 
psychological barrier in adopting new technologies.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend that : 
(i) customized awareness campaigns in the form a 
comprehensive information booklet/handbook in local 
dialects/Hindi & English containing all relevant information 
such as names & details of Schemes and its benefits, contact 
nos. & email ids of local and district/regional level officers 
belonging to Agriculture, Fertilizers, Irrigation & Storage 
Infrastructure, Insurance officers/Ombudsman  as well as 
Standard Operating Procedures to be adopted in case of 
specific challenges, need to be circulated both through digital 
medium as well as in the form of physical copies to all farmers 
in the country within the shortest span of time;   
(ii) Provide SMS based services for giving real time updates 
regarding ongoing schemes in local dialects to align with the 
Agricultural calendar. Schemes related to seeds, credit, 
fertilizers may be advertised intensively during pre-sowing 
season whereas campaigns regarding pest management and 
insurance schemes could be run during the mid-season. 

97  
During post harvest, advertisement relating to MSP 
procurement, storage infrastructure facilities, insurance 
claims, loan waiver timelines can be run on both medium- 
online(digital platforms/radio/tv) as well as offline(KVK 
staff/extension workers); 
(iii) effectively utilize the reach and impact of KVKs, Farmer 
groups and Farmer Producer Organizations in dissemination 
of information  pertaining to various government schemes 
and important timelines; 
(iv) encourage State  Governments & implementation  agencies 
to use social media to share success stories, scheme 
updates and important timelines tailored to farmers’ needs; 
(v) organize and promote “KISAN MELA” in  urban/semi-urban 
areas preferably two times in a year when the agricultural 
calendar is not hectic, to create and spread awareness about 
the farmers produce in these areas especially on weekends 
to garner more footfalls; and 
(vi) assess the impact of advertisement campaigns, be it online 
or offline, through surveys or feedback mechanisms to refine

NATIONAL MISSION ON NATURAL FARMING(NMNF)/ORGANIC FARMING 
 
8. The Committee are of the view that shifting Indian agriculture, which 
is deeply entrenched in the "Green Revolution" mindset of chemical inputs, 
requires a delicate balance of disincentivizing chemicals and incentivizing 
natural alternatives. The Committee feel that by providing a  direct cash 
incentive of around Rs.12000-15000/- per hectare, to farmers growing 
Natural& Organic produce, for the first three years to compensate for 
potential yield loss, may go a long way in promoting Natural/Organic 
Farming. This acts as "Payment for Ecosystem Services" for keeping the 
soil and water chemical-free. 
The Committee recommend that to make Natural & Organic Farming  a 
success, the government must move from a "Supply-Push" model for 
making fertilizers available to a "Demand-Pull" model for natural produce.  
Farmers need to be given an option to get cash equivalent to the amount of 
subsidy spent on Chemical fertilizers  in their respective farmlands through 
Direct Benefit Transfer(DBT).  Proper checks and balances including 
checking of samples of Soil Health need to be added to ensure 
transparency and accountability. Institutions such as Food Corporation of 
India(FCI), NAFED etc. needs to be directed to a mandatorily procure a 
certain percentage of Natural and Organic Products from Farmers/FPOs to 

99  
give boost to Natural & Organic Farming. The Department in consultation 
with Department of Food & Consumer Affairs also launch a “Bharat 
Natural” brand with select cereals with distinct identity for Natural and 
Organic Products by offering a premium price to consumers initially. By 
giving farmers an option of replacing subsidy on chemical fertilizers with 
transition grants and premium market access, the government can make 
Natural & Organic Farming not just an ecological choice, but an 
economically superior one for our farmers. The Committee also 
recommend the Department to prioritize  promoting native seeds, which are 
of superior grade — climate resilient and nutrient-rich for sustainable 
farming. These should be made readily available to farmers nationwide 
through Seed banks, Farmer Cooperatives, National Seeds Corporation 
and relevant agencies of State Agriculture Departments. The Committee 
further recommend that a National Board for Jackfruit, Tamarind and 
Jamun may be formed to fully tap their export potential  and generate 
prosperity to  lakhs of farmers. 
 
PRADHAN MANTRI FASAL BIMA YOJANA(PMFBY) 
 
 
9. The Committee note that Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) 
was launched in 2016 to provide financial support to farmers in the event 

100  
of crop failure and since then, it has removed the capping on premiums and 
lowered farmer premium rates. The Committee feel that Post-Harvest 
Losses (PHL) component may require further attention under the scheme. 
The flaws in area approach in PMFBY needs to be rectified to protect 
farmers. The data regarding yield of crops is still largely collected through 
manual Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs), which are slow, labour intensive 
and prone to human error or manipulation. Due to the delay in conducting 
CCEs and submitting data, claim settlements often happen months after 
the damage, sometimes even in the next season. This delays in getting 
instant relief for the farmer. Post-harvest losses is currently restricted only 
to crops kept in "cut and spread" condition in the field, which is a very small 
and narrow window.  The definition in PMFBY must be expanded to include 
losses occurring during pre and post harvest crops damaged due to 
lightning, fire, hailstorms, stray or wild animals, rodent & locust infestation 
irrespective of the percentage. Further, losses incurred during 
transportation, threshing, and temporary storage at the farm level, in gunny 
bags or open courtyards for up to four weeks after harvest may also be 
covered.  A "Crop Losses Reporting App" needs to be mandated  in the 
guidelines where farmers can upload geo-tagged photos of damaged 
harvested produce within 48 hours of the event subsequently followed by 

101  
assessment of damage by drones which will expedite the claim process 
faster. 
The Committee recommend that Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana 
need to become a truly comprehensive one to usher into a latest version of 
itself, by evolving from a "Crop Yield Scheme" to a "Farm Income 
Protection Scheme"  and for this to materialize, a shift from “Yield 
insurance” to “Value Chain insurance” needs to be adopted. and include 
Post-Harvest Losses by using a blend of technology such as drones& 
digital apps for assessment and actuarial reforms to cover the extended 
storage period post harvest. A “Post Harvest Clause” may be inserted into 
PMFBY to include losses from fire, natural calamities, losses occurring 
during transportation, threshing, and temporary storage at the farm level,  
kept in gunny bags or open courtyards for up to four weeks after harvest 
to enlarge the existing safety net. 
 
FARMER PRODUCER ORGANISATIONS 
 
10.  The Committee are of the view that Farmer Producer Organizations 
(FPOs) have massive potential to transform the landscape of Indian 
Agriculture. FPOs are central to the government's strategy to enhance 
farmer income, as they aggregate small and marginal farmers to achieve 
economies of scale. The Committee feel that while the formation of FPOs 

102  
has been rapid, their functionality and sustainability remain major 
challenges. 
Most FPOs are new and hence, have less assets. Banks are hesitant 
to lend to them without collateral, and the available Credit Guarantee 
Fund(CGF) covers only a fraction of the working capital needs. The Central 
Sector Scheme promises equity grants up to ₹15 lakh to match farmer 
contributions, but delays in release severely cause issues  the FPO's initial 
working capital. FPOs are typically managed by farmer-directors who 
possess agricultural knowledge but often lack business management 
skills. FPOs often lack access to aggregation centers, sorting/grading 
units, and cold storage. Without these, they are forced to sell raw produce 
immediately after harvest, missing the opportunity for price arbitrage. 
The  Committee recommend that the focus of the Government  should 
shift to handholding the FPOs during the first 5 years to ensure that  they 
become engines of rural prosperity and the work done  to provide the initial 
push through grants and other support, does not go unrewarded. 
 
KRISHI VIGYAN KENDRAS(KVK) 
 
11. The Committee are of the view that Krishi Vigyan Kendras(KVK) form 
the bedrock of India’s agricultural extension system and needs to be 
strengthened as act as frontline demonstration hubs, resource centres and 

103  
one stop platform for sustainable agricultural development. 
 The Committee recommend that each district of the country must be 
provided with at least one KVK for faster dissemination of agricultural 
knowledge and provide handholding support in latest technologies to 
farmers/farmer groups. The Committee also recommend that same farmers 
should not keep getting enrolled in the Training workshops conducted by 
KVKs but all farmers need to get at least one chance in a year to update 
themselves in the programmes being conducted by KVKs. The Committee 
also recommend that KVKs need to work in close tandem with the State 
Government/UTs and inform public representatives like MPs, MLAs, 
Corporators etc. regarding their upcoming programmes, events well in 
advance for wider outreach. The Committee further recommend that KVKs 
need to promote cultivation of native seeds among farmers especially in 
drought prone and ecologically sensitive areas. 
 
STRENGHTENING OF e-NATIONAL AGRICULTURE MARKETS (e-NAM) 
 
12. The Committee are of the considered view that e-NAM need to  shift 
from price discovery to seamless trade execution. The Committee   strongly 
feel that financial interests of farmers may be protected from buyers at all 
costs and the Department may ensure that farmers are provided all the 
requisite handholding and other assistance during developing digital 

104  
literacy to enable them avail benefits under the scheme. 
The Committee recommend that a Single Unified Trading License 
valid across all e-NAM mandis be mandated to eliminate state barriers and 
broaden the buyer base. The Committee also recommend to deploy 
automated quality assaying machines in mandis and give priority to 
issuance of standardized digital certificates for distant buyers to trust the 
produce without physical inspection. The Committee also recommend to 
enforce a strict escrow based settlement mechanism to guarantee timely 
payment to farmers and to link e-NAM with relevant platforms to ensure 
affordable, real-time transport solutions for inter-state movement of 
produce. 
 
EMPHASIS ON SOIL HEALTH 
 
13. The Committee feel that Soil health is the main edifice of agricultural 
productivity and food security.  The Committee feel that the time lag 
between sample collection of soil and delivery of Soil Health Card(Soil 
Health Card) needs to be reduced to less than a week. Presently,  by the 
time the  Soil health card is received, the cropping season may have already 
begun or passed, rendering the advice useless for that cycle. The grid size  
issues also needs to be sorted  out as  a farm within a grid of 10 
hectares(rainfed) or 2.5 hectares(irrigated) may have different nutrient 

105  
profiles. There is a shortage of laboratories, leading to outsourcing to 
private players. The quality of analysis varies between labs due to a lack of 
standardized equipment and quality control protocols. On many occasions, 
the Soil Health Card issued miss details regarding secondary nutrients 
such as Sulphur and micronutrients such as Zinc, Boron, Iron which are 
the  limiting factors in the soil today due to intensive farming. The technical 
jargon on the cards also needs to be simplified to the maximum extent 
possible so that small and marginal farmers can easily decipher the 
recommendations made.  The availability of micronutrients such as Zinc, 
Gypsum  and so on also needs to be made  on regular basis across the 
Cooperative Stores.  
The Committee recommend that dynamic measures need to be taken 
to increase carbon content in the soil across the country and geo tagging 
of soil samples need to be done to create a geospatial database which will 
help in creating precise "Soil Fertility Maps" for districts, moving away from 
generic grid sampling to farm-specific analysis.  Testing for biological 
parameters (organic carbon, microbial biomass) and physical parameters 
(soil structure, water holding capacity) also needs to be included 
mandatorily in Soil Health Card. The Committee also recommend that Near-
Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) and satellite imagery to map soil properties 

106  
need to be completed across the country at the earliest years as this would 
allow for larger area coverage with higher accuracy. The Soil Health Card 
needs to be simplified in common terms   and over a period of time replace 
it with a Digital App in areas where internet connectivity is good so that real 
time nutrient recommendations based on GPS-tagged soil samples.  
Extension workers also need to be trained to interpret Soil Health Cards 
and counsel farmers while distributing them. Soil health data should be 
integrated with the PM Fasal Bima Yojana as healthy soils reduce crop risk 
and farmers with good soil health scores could be offered lower insurance 
premiums, turning soil conservation for farmers into an additional revenue 
stream. The Committee feel that the Department need to maintain subsidy 
on drip and sprinkler irrigation  as this lowers farmers’ initial investment in 
micro-irrigation systems and encourage faster adoption while allowing 
cultivation in water scarce areas as well as allowing precise and timely 
application of fertilizers thereby providing cost advantage especially to 
small and marginal farmers. 
 
The Committee further recommend the Department to explore ways 
and methods to implement subsurface drainage systems existing in 
Belgavi in Karnataka, in water logging areas & coastal areas  across the 
country  to  effectively combat excess surplus subsoil water for disposal 

107  
into surface drains which will transform underproductive lands, enhance 
soil health and  increase farmer prosperity. 
  

108  
 
NATIONAL SEEDS CORPORATION 
 
14. The Committee note that National Seeds Corporation (NSC) is the 
apex body for seed production in India and has played a historic role in the 
Green Revolution. It now faces competition from a vibrant private sector 
and hence, it requires a strategic roadmap to transform itself to meet the 
existing and upcoming challenges. The Committee are of the considered 
view that Upper Price Ceiling of Seeds needs to be implemented by the 
Department to protect farmers and their legitimate interests. 
The Committee feel that NSC needs to invest in the state of the art  
machinery for seed production and packaging & establish climate-
controlled warehouses to prevent seed deterioration, implement RFID 
(Radio Frequency Identification) and Blockchain technology for real-time 
tracking of seed lots from production to the retailer, ensuring traceability 
and checking counterfeiting. NSC need to use satellite imagery and drones 
to monitor seed crops in real-time to ensure isolation distances and 
rouging (removal of off-type plants) are done effectively, addressing the 
issue of genetic impurity. NSC also needs to promote native seeds to 
farmers across the country to strengthen crop resilience, maintain 
ecological balance, secure and enrich crop diversity. NSC is heavily tilted 
towards cereals such as wheat, paddy whereas the market is shifting 

109  
towards horticulture, millets, and hybrids. NSC also needs to shore up its 
last mile delivery to boost sales. 
The Committee recommend that National Seeds Corporation (NSC) 
needs to transform its identity from a "Government Supplier" to a " 
futuristic, global-grade seed entity " by combining public sector trust and 
reach with the efficiency and technology of private sector. The Committee 
also recommend that NSC should ensure that Indian farmers have access 
to affordable, high-quality, and climate-resilient seeds, even in areas with 
sub-optimal connectivity, in securing the nation's food future. 
 
NATIONAL HORTICULTURE BOARD(NHB) 
 
15. The Committee note that National Horticulture Board (NHB) plays an 
important role in developing Post-Harvest infrastructure (PHI) and 
promoting high-tech Horticulture. The Committee feel that NHB needs to 
engage itself more proactively and act as a catalyst to transform the 
landscape of Post Harvest Infrastructure and high-tech Horticulture. 
The Committee recommend that NHB needs to completely digitize its 
operations, focus on integrated value chains, and link horticulture directly 
to export markets. For the farmers who are not tech savvy, options to need 
to be given to them to submit their application in physical copies. The 
administrative processes in NHB schemes also needs to be streamlined to 

110  
expedite approvals and 100% of subsidies need to be transferred directly 
to the beneficiary's bank account, removing intermediaries and state-level 
bottlenecks. NHB should mandate the creation of integrated "Pack Houses" 
linked to cold storages and transport. NHB schemes need to be aligned 
with Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) to provide interest subvention, 
making capital cheaper for entrepreneurs setting up processing units. The 
Committee also recommend that NHB should register Geographical 
Indication (GI) tags for horticultural produce and create an umbrella brand 
for Indian agro produce for international marketing and also promote bio 
fortified varieties. 
 
VIKSIT BHARAT-2047 
 
16.  The Committee recommend that in order to visualize the dream of a 
developed India- Viksit Bharat by 2047, the roadmap requires shifting from 
a "production-centric" approach to an "income-centric" and 
"sustainability-centric" model. Artificial Intelligence needs to be integrated 
with precision farming to optimize input use such as water, fertilizers etc. 
thereby reducing costs & environmental damage and drones need to be 
utilized for crop monitoring purposes.  The Committee also recommend 
that a unified digital ecosystem connecting land records, soil health, 

111  
weather forecasts, and market prices needs to be implemented. This data 
should be available to farmers on a single smartphone app to support real-
time decision-making. Shift from "per acre" irrigation to "per drop" 
irrigation needs to be done and Micro-irrigation (drip/sprinkler) must 
become the norm, covering 100% of irrigated areas. For this purpose, inter-
departmental convergence may be strengthened between the Department 
of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare(DAFW) and the Department of Water 
Resources, River Development & Ganga Rejuvenation under the Ministry 
of Jal Shakti. Steps may also be taken to enhance participation at the 
grassroots level through the involvement of village-level Water Committees 
at the Gram Sabha Level. The Committee further recommend that Indian 
farmers  need to be positioned as providers of "Carbon Credits" thereby 
creating an additional revenue stream for them. The Department should 
also establish specialized training centres for modern techniques like 
hydroponics, aquaponics, and drone piloting at block level in the country. 
A "Green Revolution 2.0" specifically for the Eastern and North-Eastern 
states, needs to be launched to bridge the regional productivity gap, 
focusing on horticulture and pulses. FPOs need to be transformed as 
centres of Global Trade completely transforming the profile of the 
Annadata into a prosperous individual. Most importantly, by 2047, 

112  
agriculture needs to be turned into a sustainable, profitable and resilient 
business thereby catapulting India to lead the Ivy league of nations. 
 
EDUCATIONAL SUPPORT FOR CHILDREN OF SMALL AND SEMI-MEDIUM 
FARMERS  
 
17. The Committee observes that small and semi-medium farmers form 
the backbone of India’s agricultural economy. However, many farming 
households continue to face financial distress due to low and uncertain 
farm incomes, rising input costs and indebtedness.  
In view of this situation, the Committee is of the considered opinion 
that the State must extend stronger social and educational support to the 
families of farmers. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the 
Government of India, through the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare 
in coordination with the Ministry of Education, introduce a National 
Scholarship Scheme for the Children of Small and Semi-Medium Farmers, 
with special provisions for the children of farmers affected by extreme 
financial distress. 
 
18. The Committee recommend that before concluding any bilateral or 
multilateral agreements which affect the farming sector, appropriate 
consultations may be held with the relevant stakeholders. 

113  
 
SUBSIDY ON EV TRACTORS 
 
 
19. The Committee feel that EV (Electric Vehicle) tractors are vital for 
sustainable farming as they cut diesel emissions significantly thereby 
promoting a greener planet with lesser carbon emissions. They also 
promote energy independence via solar charging and align them with 
India's net-zero goals. 
The Committee recommend that proportionate subsidies may be 
given on EV Tractors to that of Diesel Tractors to make them economically 
feasible and boost their acceptance among the farmers especially Small 
and Marginal farmers. The Committee also recommend that infrastructure 
relating to EV charging facilities may also be scaled up in rural areas to 
make EV tractors popular among the farmers.

4 Pg.88-89 CHANGE OF NOMENCLATURE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
AGRICULTURE & FARMERS WELFARE TO DEPARTMENT OF 
AGRICULTURE, FARMERS & FARM LABOURERS WELFARE 
 
    The Committee are of the considered view that the nomenclature of 
the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare of the Union 
Government may be changed to Department of Agriculture, Farmers & 
Farm Labourers Welfare. This would not be merely a semantic change 
but would represent and enable a paradigm shift in policy focus. Till now, 
the focus of the Department has mostly been on production and yield of 
agricultural produce but the proposed change in nomenclature will also 
focus on the human resources involved in the production and recognise 
the unsung efforts of "invisible hands" of Indian agriculture, Farm or 
Landless labourers. This inclusion of “Farm Labourers” in the official 
nomenclature will send a strong message that the Government grants 
official recognition to the Farm Labourers and acknowledge their 
immense contribution in the agricultural ecosystem ensuring that they 
do not remain on the margins of policy benefits. 
 
The Committee feel that revising the nomenclature of the Department 
and adding the term “Farm Labourers” to the title, offers several potential 
benefits to this vulnerable section of Farm Labourers, including paving 
the way for their inclusion in specific social security schemes such as 
pension funds, health insurance (under Ayushman Bharat), and 
maternity benefits tailored specifically for agricultural labourers, distinct 
from general labour welfare. 
 
      The Committee recommend that the proposed change of 
nomenclature of the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare of the 
Union Government at present to Department of Agriculture, Farmers & 
Farm Labourers Welfare may be done to send a clear signal that the 
Government accords the same dignity and status to Farm Labourers as 
that of Land-owning farmers and that the sweat and toil of Farm 
Labourers is immensely valued by the nation. This would also broaden 

188  
the vision of the Department which manages crops at present to the one 
which would be responsible for the protection of the entire human 
resources involved in ensuring food security of the country and aligns 
with the broader goals of Social Justice and Equity as enshrined in the 
Constitution. The new change would also ensure that this vulnerable 
group of Farm Labourers, majority of whom belong to SC/ST/OBC, are 
protected during agrarian crises as they are the ones who primarily lose 
their employment during such hardships. This change in nomenclature 
would also enable the creation of specific budgetary support for skill 
development of Farm Labourers helping them to acquire new skill sets 
in operation of latest agricultural machines & gadgets, thereby 
increasing their earning potential. The Committee further recommend 
that the Department should explore ways and methods in which 
schemes like PM-KISAN may be extended to Farm Labourers. This 
would significantly play an important role in curbing distress migration 
from rural to urban areas by Farm labourers, as this workforce can be 
retained in rural areas through employment guarantees and livelihood 
diversification. This will facilitate a broad-based growth across the 
country.” 
 
The Committee were of the view that detailed discussion with all 
relevant stakeholders including different government departments 
including Ministry of Labour may be done and hence, the matter of 
change of nomenclature may be deferred. However, the Committee 
were of the view that the above narration may be replaced with the 
following- 
 
IMPORTANCE OF FARM LABOURER AND THE NEED FOR THEIR 
INCLUSION IN THE MANDATE OF DEPARTMENT OF 
AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE  
 
     The Committee are of the view that Farm Labourers are an 
important component of the Agricultural ecosystem in the country. 
Farm Labourers face unique & diverse challenges which are totally 
different than faced by any other class of Labourers including 
industrial labourers. In the current welfare measures being 
implemented by the Ministry right focus is being accorded for 
farmer welfare, but the labour which provides the necessary 
workforce in the agriculture fields is unable to reap the benefit as 
they do not own the land which they till.  The Committee feel that 
the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) should 
make concerted efforts for identifying the unique challenges being 
faced by the labourers working on the farms. The Committee 
further note that while the   Ministry of Labour is the nodal Ministry 
to implement the welfare schemes for the labour class in the 
country, however farm labour being a distinct category and are 
different from industrial labour. As such, the agriculture labour are 
not identified as workmen/industrial labour and they are unable to 

189  
reap the benefits being accorded to industrial labourers viz. 
Medical Care, Insurance and social Security. In this backdrop the 
Committee recommend that the Ministry Agriculture & Farmers 
Welfare (DA&FW) should consider to widen the ambit of 
component of Farmer Welfare and should include the welfare of 
Farm Labourers within its scope. The Committee also recommend 
that the Ministry needs to identify programmes, schemes, 
missions etc for their inclusion in specific social security schemes 
such as pension funds, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana, 
and maternity benefits tailored specifically for agricultural 
labourers.

REPORT 
 
PART- I 
 
CHAPTER - I 
 
Introductory 
 
1.1 The Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) was established in 
the Ministry of Agriculture in December 1973. DARE coordinates and promotes Agricultural 
Research and Education in the country.  
Mandate of DARE 
i. Fundamental, applied and operational research and higher education including 
coordination of such research and higher education. 
ii. Coordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education 
or research and scientific and technical institutions. 
iii. International cooperation and assistance in the field of agricultural research 
and education including relations with foreign and international agricultural 
research and education institutions and organizations. 
 
It has the following four autonomous bodies under its administrative control: 
 Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), New Delhi 
 Central Agricultural University (CAU), Imphal  
 Dr. Rajendra Prasad Central Agricultural University, Pusa, Bihar 
 Rani Laxmi Bai Central Agricultural University, Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh 
 
1.2 The DARE provides the necessary government linkages for the Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research (ICAR), the premier research Organisation for coordinating, guiding 
and managing research, education and extension in Agriculture including horticulture, 
fisheries and animal sciences in the entire country. Besides, it has Agricultural Scientists 
Recruitment Board (ASRB) as an Attached Office and Agrinnovate India Limited (AgIn), a 
Government of India enterprise under its control. 
 

2 
 
1.3 The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) is an apex scientific research 
Organization for planning, promotion, execution and coordination of agriculture research and 
education in the country. Formerly known as the Imperial Council of Agricultural Research, 
it was established on 16 July, 1929 as a registered society under the Societies Registration 
Act, 1860 on the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Agriculture. It was 
reorganized in 1965 and again in 1973, with its Headquarters located in Krishi Bhawan, New 
Delhi with support facilities in Krishi Anusandhan Bhawan 1 and 2 and NASC Complex, 
Pusa, New Delhi. It functions at a national level through networks of institutes, projects (All-
India Coordinated/ Networks) comprising of eight Subject Matter Divisions operating 8 
Central Sector Schemes and has linkages with State Agriculture Universities and other 
Departments of the Central and State Governments. 
 
Organizational Set up of ICAR 
 
1.4 The ICAR, as a vibrant organization, continues to generate technologies for 
sustainable development of Agriculture. The ICAR is the guiding and monitoring entity of the 
country for National Agriculture Research System (NARS) consisting of 113 Research and 
Educational Institutes, 77 Agricultural Universities and 731 Krishi Vigyan Kendras spread 
across the country having responsibility of developing technologies in various fields of 
agriculture and allied sectors. 
There are eight Subject Matter Divisions, viz. i) Crop Science, ii) Natural Resource 
Management iii) Horticultural Science, iv) Animal Science, v) Fisheries Science, vi) 
Agricultural Engineering vii) Agricultural Education, and viii) Agricultural Extension and they 
are entrusted with the overall responsibility for the preparation, scrutiny, review, and 
technical supervision and guidance of the research schemes, educational and extension 
programs and projects within their respective disciplines. 
 
Vision of ICAR 
Advancing Agri-Food System Science, Participatory innovations, Partnership and 
enhanced Stakeholders’ Capacity for building resilient Food, Land and Water Systems to 
ensure nutritious and healthy food for all while protecting, conserving and restoring 
ecosystem even in a climate crisis. 
 

3 
 
Mandate of ICAR: 
 Plan, Undertake, Coordinate and Promote Research and Technology Development 
for Sustainable Agriculture. 
 Aid, Impart and Coordinate Agricultural Education to enable Quality Human 
Resource Development. 
 Frontline Extension for technology application, adoption, knowledge management 
and capacity development for agri-based rural development. 
 Policy, Cooperation and Consultancy in Agricultural Research, Education and 
Extension. 
 
Goal of ICAR 
 
1.5 The goal of ICAR is to promote sustainable and inclusive agricultural growth and 
development in the country by interfacing education, research and extension initiatives 
complemented with efficient and effective institutional, infrastructure and policy support, for 
ensuring livelihood and environmental security. 
ICAR has rationalized its earlier Central Sector Schemes into 8 Central Sector 
Schemes. The list of the Schemes is as follows:

considering prevailing weather forecast and fluctuations. Presently, more than 3 crore 
farmers are receiving agromet advisories through the Gramin Krishi Mausam Seva. The

on seasonal crop selection depending upon the climatic suitability for the particular region.

region specific, high yielding, climate resilient crop varieties regularly along with matching 
package of practices as per the need of the farming community. Out of 3236 varieties 
developed since 2014 to 2025, 2996 varieties are climate resilient and are tolerant to one 
or more biotic and/or abiotic stresses, amongst which 587 are extreme climate tolerant 
varieties. Out of these 587 varieties, 341 are drought tolerant / less water consuming 
varieties; 89 are flood tolerant / water logging tolerant varieties; 80 are salinity / sodicity 
tolerant varieties, 59 are heat stress tolerant varieties and 18 are cold tolerant varieties and 
developed using the precision phenotyping tools. A total of 286 climate resilient 
technologies have been developed for the benefit of stakeholders/ farmers of 22 states and 
3 Union Territories (UTs). The climate resilient technologies including crop varieties, 
intercropping systems, conservation agriculture, crop diversification, agroforestry systems, 
zero till drill sowing of wheat to escape terminal heat stress, alternate methods of rice 
cultivation (system of rice intensification, aerobic rice and direct seeded rice), in-situ 
moisture conservation etc. have been disseminated among the farmers/ stakeholders in 
151 vulnerable districts across the country.

productivity, production etc. The Department also put emphasis on agricultural 
technologies reach to farmers/ end users through extension programs such as 
Smart, Participatory, Expeditious Extension Delivery (SPEED) Model, Skilling & 
Attracting Rural Youth for Agri-based Livelihoods (SARAL), frontline 
demonstrations, training and skill development of farmers, entrepreneurs and 
extension workers, supply of technological inputs and advisories for different 
productions systems to farmers. The Department initiatives and action plan are 
given as under: 
1. Establishment of MELIA Unit (Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning, Impact 
Assessment): Data driven decision making  
2. ICAR Communication Policy and Strategy  
3. ICAR Research Data Management Policy 
4. ICAR Gender Strategy for National Agricultural Research, Education and 
Extension System 
5. Agriculture for Health  
6. Nutritional security through New age breeding and management 
7. Climate reliance technologies and practices 
8. Mission for Cotton Productivity (Kapas Kanti)  
9. National Mission on High Yielding Seeds 
10. Genebank for Crops Germplasm (National Safety Copy Plant Genebank) 
11. Smart mechanization and precision agriculture 
12. Smart precision aquaculture through sensor-automated and AI-driven 
autonomous monitoring  
13. Bharat-VISTAAR (Virtually Integrated System to Access Agricultural 
Resources) is a multilingual AI-based digital platform 
14. Strengthening, Agri-Business and Start-up Ecosystem  
15. Last Mile Delivery of Technology through Convergence Mode 
16. Human Resource Development in Agriculture and Allied Sectors 
17. Value Chain and Global outreach’ 
 
3.5 When the Committee specifically asked about the challenges/constraints the 
Department is facing or likely to face in achieving the targets fixed/set as part of Viksit Bharat 
by 2047, the Department stated: 
‘The Department has stagnated allocations for last several years by the Ministry of 
Finance, moreover allocations are further reduced at RE stage. An allocation of one 
percent of Agricultural GDP is required for R&D in Agriculture to achieve the desired 
targets of the Department for the VIKSIT Bharat-2047.’ 

49 
 
PART-II 
 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
1. The Committee note that the Department of Agricultural Research and 
Education (DARE) sought an allocation of Rs. 11427.51 crore in BE for the year 2026-
27, it got Rs. 9967.40 crore which is 0.19% of total Outlay (BE) of Rs. 5347315.00 crore 
of Government of India for the year.  This allocation is, however, lower than the 
allocations of Rs. 10466.39 crore made in BE 2025-26 and Rs. 10280.83 crore made in 
RE 2025-26.  The Committee also note that the proportion (in percentage terms) of the 
Budgetary Allocation (BE) made in favour of the Department out of the total BE 
allocation of the Government of India has declined from 0.24% in the year 2021-22 to 
0.19% in 2026-27.  During the last three years, the allocation to the Department was 
0.21% of the total outlay (BE) of the Government of India. The Committee have been 
apprised by the Department that the present allocation in BE 2026-27 shall impact the 
schemes and programs planned by various subject matter divisions and over all 
working of the Institutes. The Committee have also been apprised that India’s public 
agricultural R&D spending is about 0.5-0.6% of Agri-GDP against the global average 
of ~0.93%. 
 
The Committee are of the firm opinion that further strengthening of Agriculture 
and Allied Sector is imperative for economic resilience, improving the livelihood of 
millions, promoting rural prosperity, ensuring food and nutrition security and driving 
inclusive growth in the country. The Department of Agricultural Research and 
Education (DARE) and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), being the 

50 
 
premier research organization, play crucial role in strengthening Agriculture and 
Allied sector by addressing the priority and challenging issues through Research, 
Education and Extension. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Government to 
consider increasing the allocation for the Department for making Research, Education 
and Extension Ecosystem of Agriculture and Allied Sector strong, robust and modern 
in the country. 
 
UTILIZATION OF FUND UNDER CAPITAL SECTION (CAPITAL OUTLAY ON OTHER 
GENERAL ECONOMIC SERVICES) 
 
2. The Committee note that Rs. 10.41 crore and Rs. 6.50 crore were allocated in 
BE 2023-24 and BE 2024-25 respectively under ‘Capital Section (Capital Outlay on 
other General Economic Services)’ of the Department which were reduced to  
Rs. 9.96 crore and Rs. 3.82 crore in RE of the respective years. However, the 
Department was able to utilize only Rs. 3.39 crore in the year 2023-24 and Rs. 3.15 
crore in 2024-25. The Committee also note that the allocation of Rs. 4.33 crore under 
this head in BE 2025-26 was reduced to Rs. 2.49 crore in RE 2025-26 and till January 
2026, the Department has been able to utilize only Rs. 1.0346 crore i.e. 23.89% of BE 
allocation and 41.55% of RE allocation for the year. 
 
The Committee are of the considered view that the allocated amount under any 
head of the Department should be properly and optimally utilized for the intended 
purpose(s).  The Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to analyse the 
reasons for under-utilization of allocated fund under ‘Capital Section’ and 
consequently devise proper strategy and planning for optimum utilization of allocated 
fund in a time-bound manner. 

51 
 
ALLOCATION UNDER SCHEME HEAD 
 
3.  The Committee note that out of the total allocation (BE) of Rs. 9967.40 crore to 
the Department (DARE) for the year 2026-27, Rs. 2830.12 crore has been allocated 
under Scheme Head which constitutes around 28.39% of the total allocation. The 
allocation under Scheme Head in BE 2026-27 (Rs. 2830.12 crore) is 389.10 crore less 
than the allocation of Rs. 3219.22 crore in BE 2025-26 and Rs. 97.42 crore less than 
the allocation of Rs. 2927.54 crore in RE 2025-26.  The Committee also note that the 
Department has sought/proposed Rs. 3015.17 crore only under Scheme Head for  
BE 2026-27 which marks the first year of the 16th Finance Cycle.  The Committee have 
been apprised that as a result of reduced allocation under Scheme Head in  
RE 2025-26, the Department had to prioritize its research and development activities 
and optimize administrative expenses to achieve the desired goals and objectives. 
Also, programs and activities of low emergent type were deferred for the coming 
financial years. Further, due to inadequate allocation in BE 2026-27, similar strategies 
will be adopted during this year too. 
 
The Committee are of considered view that allocation of adequate financial 
resources is imperative for developing of robust R&D ecosystem for Agriculture and 
Allied Sector to achieve the desired result. The Committee, therefore, recommend the 
Department to take up the matter of enhancing the allocation under Scheme Head with 
the Ministry of Finance. 
 
  

52 
 
Natural Resource Management and National Innovations in Climate Resilient  
Agriculture (NICRA) 
 
4. The Committee note that Natural Resource Management and National 
Innovations in Climate Resilient Agriculture (NICRA) Division has been allocated Rs. 
232.05 crore in BE 2026-27 which is marginally higher than the allocations of Rs. 
229.09 crore made in BE 2025-26 and Rs. 198.09 crore in RE 2025-26.  The Committee 
also note that the Division has utilized 83.60% (till 31st January, 2026) of the allocation 
in RE 2025-26. The Committee appreciate that the Division has developed and 
disseminated the climate resilient technologies including crop varieties, 
intercropping systems, conservation agriculture, crop diversification, agroforestry 
systems, zero till drill sowing of wheat to escape terminal heat stress, alternate 
methods of rice cultivation (System of rice intensification, aerobic rice and direct 
seeded rice), in-situ moisture conservation etc. among the farmers/stakeholders in 
151 vulnerable districts across the country.  It is also quite commendable that the 
deployment of climate resilient varieties and other technologies led to enhanced 
production even during the abnormal years of 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 
and the fluctuations in crop production have decreased over the years. The 
Committee, however, emphasise the importance of continuing and further 
strengthening such efforts, particularly in view of the likely increase in the frequency 
and intensity of climate change, as well as emerging biotic (pests, diseases, weeds) 
and abiotic stresses (drought, high temperatures, salinity, acidity) in the future.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to ensure sufficient allocation and 
optimal utilization of the allocated fund to the Division and give priority to Research 
for development of location-specific, cost-effective, eco-friendly Climate Resilient 

53 
 
Practices and Technologies suitable for different agro-ecological regions and their 
dissemination and demonstration on large scale in the country so as to 
minimize/contain the adverse impact of climate changes and other constraints and 
promote sustainability in Agriculture. 
 
AGRICULTURAL ENGINEERING 
 
 
5. The Committee note that Rs. 96.50 crore has been allocated to the Agricultural 
Engineering Division in BE 2026-27 which is marginally more than the allocations of 
Rs. 95.74 crore in BE 2025-26 and Rs. 89.00 crore in RE 2025-26. The Committee also 
note that the Division has utilized 73.66% (Rs. 65.66 crore) of allocation made in RE 
2025-26 till January 2026.  The Committee appreciate that the Division has contributed 
immensely in development, demonstration and commercialization of new 
machines/equipment/technologies for improving pre and post production 
mechanization of different crops/crop operations, development of process protocols 
and value-added food, fibre and other agricultural allied products and reorientation of 
research projects for development of machine/technologies with fusion of 
sensors/artificial intelligence. The Committee are of the view that farm mechanization 
is necessary for enhancing efficiency in agricultural operations/activities and 
reducing drudgery on human beings, but economic viability of any 
machine/technology also needs to be assessed before recommending for its 
widespread adoption. The Committee note that in some instances, the purchase of 
tractors by small and marginal farmers has placed additional financial pressure on 
them.  The Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to take steps for 
promoting need-based mechanization and developing appropriate, affordable 

54 
 
machinery/ equipment/ technologies, supported by R&D and considering the fact that 
majority of farmers in the country are small and marginal having small and fragmented 
landholdings. 
 
CROP SCIENCE 
 
6.  The Committee note that Rs. 969.50 crore has been allocated to Crop Science 
Division which is marginally higher than the allocations made in BE & RE 2025-26 (Rs. 
965.46 crore).  The Committee also note that high yielding varieties of Field Crops 
developed by the ICAR have led to increase in productivity and production of these 
crops, yet there remains substantial potential to enhance agricultural productivity.   
Yields across several crops including cereals, maize soybeans and pulses, continue 
to trail global averages. Besides, progress remains uneven across States and crops 
in improved seed availability and varietal replacement rates. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to optimally and effectively 
utilize the allocation made to this Division and lay emphasis on preserving and 
developing indigenous crop varieties for better productivity and yield while retaining 
originality in taste, flavour, shelf life, nutrients, etc.  The Committee also recommend 
the Department to develop, disseminate and popularize agricultural practices for 
production of crops from natural/intrinsic strength of the soil avoiding use of 
chemical fertilizers, pesticides etc. 
  

55 
 
HORTICULTURE SCIENCE 
 
 
7.  The Committee note that Rs. 220.00 crore has been allocated to Horticulture 
Science Division in BE 2026-27 which is lower than the allocations made in BE 2025-
26 (Rs. 318.91 crore) and RE 2025-26 (Rs. 262.91 crore).  The Committee also note that 
Horticulture sector has witnesses tremendous progress and is playing an important 
role in promoting income diversification, nutritional security and more resilient 
agricultural growth. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to 
continue to lay emphasis on growth of productivity and production of Horticultural 
Crops in the country. 
 
ANIMAL SCIENCE 
 
8. The Committee note that Rs. 416.95 crore has been allocated to Animal Science 
Division in BE 2026-27 which is quite lower than the allocations of Rs. 504.04 crore in 
BE 2025-26 and Rs. 417.04 crore in RE 2025-26.  The Committee also note that the 
Division has utilized 78% of the allocated funds for the year 2025-26 till January 2026.  
The Committee have been apprised that the ICAR’s research on veterinary biologicals 
has led to successful eradication of important animal diseases and the Department is 
working on development of new generation vaccines, identification of indigenous 
livestocks, genome editing and animal genomics studies etc. for improved animal 
health and production in the country.  The Committee have also been apprised about 
demand-supply gaps in green fodder, dry fodder and concentrates leading to 
persistent shortages and quality constraints of feed and fodder affecting the livestock 
nutrition. Considering livestock sector as an important growth engine and key 
contributors to enhancing farm income, the Committee recommend the Department 

56 
 
to take steps for ensuring feed and fodder security for the animals. The Committee 
also recommend the Department for preservation and development of indigenous 
breeds for cow in view of its usefulness to the human beings and the society as a 
whole. 
 
FISHERIES SCIENCE 
 
9.  During the Study Visit of the Committee in January 2026, the Committee 
undertook an on-the-spot visit to Germplasm Resource Centre for Marine Ornamental 
Organism of ICAR – National Bureau of Fish Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBFGR) 
located at Agatti Island of Lakshadweep. The representative(s) of the Centre inter-alia 
raised issues/demands for expansion of the facility and increase in production in 
hatchery, development and making available specialized facility or packing materials 
for packing Ornamental fishes and other aquatic organisms etc. to cater the 
requirements/demands of ever-increasing tourists to Lakshadweep islands who want 
to purchase and carry them home as memento. The Committee have been apprised 
by the Department that the activities at the Centre is restricted to certain outreach 
activities intended to demonstrate the technologies pertaining to ornamental fish 
breeding and rearing and the activities could be expanded depending on the resource 
availability.  The Committee, while sympathetic to the demand of the Centre, 
recommend to the Department to make available sufficient resources for its 
expansion and the requisite packing material to cater the requirement of interested 
tourists who want to purchase and carry them home as memento. 
  

57 
 
AGRICULTURAL EXTENSION 
 
10. The Committee note that Agricultural Extension Division has been allocated Rs. 
210.00 crore in BE 2026-27 which is more than the allocations made in BE 2025-26 (Rs. 
204.23 crore) and RE 2025-26 (Rs. 182.23 crore) but less than the Actual Expenditure 
(Rs. 234.69 crore) incurred during the financial year 2024-25. During the financial year 
2025-26, the Division has utilized Rs. 144.2 crore (79% of RE allocation) as on 
20.01.2026. 
The Committee are of the view that Agricultural Extension plays a vital role in 
transferring scientific knowledge, improved technologies and sustainable agriculture 
practices to farmers, thereby enhancing productivity and resilience.  However, the 
Committee note that agricultural extension services in the country continue to face 
certain challenges relating to outreach, availability of trained personnel, and 
coordination in service delivery.  Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), which play a crucial 
role in extension activities, are yet to be established in every district of the country.  
At present, there are 731 KVKs.  While 93 districts have two KVKs each, 121 districts 
do not have a KVK.  The Committee further note that no new KVK has been opened 
during the last 3 years.  In addition, some of the existing KVKs face infrastructural 
constraints, and around 29% of the sanctioned posts across KVKs remain vacant. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to establish/open at least 
one KVK with adequate infrastructure and sufficient manpower in each district of the 
country including the Union Territories which do not have such facilities. The 
Committee also recommend the Department to make extension services at KVK more 
broad-based and inclusive so that maximum number of farmers are able to avail the 

58 
 
services.  Besides, the Committee recommend the Department to take steps /action 
for maintaining uniform standards of performance, transparency, service delivery and 
availability of financial resources across all KVKs to ensure effective and equitable 
outreach to the farming community. 
 
VIKSIT KRISHI SANKALP ABHIYAN 
 
11. The Committee have been apprised about the Viksit Krishi Sankalp Abhiyan 
which was organized in the country from May 29, 2025 to June 12, 2025.  The Abhiyan 
was organized in 725 districts by 2170 teams. 60,281 events were organized and 
140122 villages and 134.85 lakh farmers were covered.  As a result of the Abhiyan, 
more than 300 farmer-led innovations, approximately 500 researchable issues and 70 
policy inputs emerged. The Committee, while recognizing the benefits of the Abhiyan 
accrued to the farmers and Agriculture Sector recommend the Department to organize 
such Abhiyan on regular basis in the country. 
 
AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION 
 
12. The Committee note that Rs. 514.87 crore has been allocated for Agricultural 
Education in BE 2026-27 which is less than the allocations made in BE 2025-26 (Rs. 
708.94 crore) and RE 2025-26 (Rs. 645.00 crore).  The Committee also note that Rs. 
484.00 crore (approx. 75%) has been utilized till January 2026 during the financial year 
2025-26.  The Committee feel that there is a need to strengthen Agricultural Education 
in the country and the reduction in allocation for Agricultural Education would 
adversely affect it. Further, the Committee desire that the basic Agricultural Education 
may be introduced at School level to familiarize young generation with agriculture 

59 
 
activities and processes. The Committee also desire the Department to explore the 
possibility of opening agricultural college(s)/institution(s) exclusively for girls to take 
care of the requirements and sensibilities/concerns of rural areas of the country. 
 
PROVISIONS FOR SC/ST FARMERS 
 
13. The Committee note that the Department do not have any specific scheme for 
Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe sections of the society. However, the Department 
implemented Development action plan Scheduled Caste (DASC) and Development action plan 
Scheduled Tribe (DAPST) component within the scheme wherein SC/ST communities were 
supported with skill development, supply of inputs, transfer of agricultural technologies and 
knowledge to undertake agriculture and allied operations at agricultural farms and fields for 
enhancement of agricultural production and productivity. The Committee are of the view that 
Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) farmers, constituting a substantial portion of 
the nation’s agricultural population, are primarily small or marginal landholders having small 
and fragmented plots. They face significant barriers including limited access to institutional 
credit, quality inputs and advanced technology resulting in lower productivity and lower net 
returns. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Department to take steps/action to 
indicate specific requirements of the farmers belonging to these segments so that they can 
be provided with the necessary skill sets and technology application so that they too can 
benefit from the various innovations made by the Department in the agriculture sector so that 
they are not left out and the benefits of agricultural research, education and extensions 
schemes of the Department are fully availed by the SC/ST farmers for improving their 
livelihood and income. 
 
  

60 
 
VIKSIT BHARAT @ 2047 
 
14. The Committee note that the Department has set ambitious targets for various 
parameters in Agriculture and Allied Sector’s research to be achieved by 2047 as part 
of Viksit Bharat and has been making sincere efforts to achieve them. The Committee 
are quite hopeful that the Department would surmount the challenges of climate 
change, declining arable land and water resources, emerging biotic 
(pests/diseases/weeds) and abiotic stresses (drought, high temperatures, salinity, 
acidity), market and trade uncertainty and global conflicts and achieve the set targets. 
The Committee also agree with the concerns of the Department about stagnated 
allocations for last several years and subsequent reductions at RE stage and, 
therefore, recommend the Department to pursue with the Ministry of Finance for an 
allocation of one percent of Agricultural GDP for R&D in Agriculture so as not to allow 
fund constraints come in the way of achieving the targets.
